opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to separate two questions: what synthetic data can do in principle, and where the bottlenecks are today.

In principle, I'm quite optimistic. Synthetic data scales without limit. Once you have a good simulator and good assets, generating a billion trajectories costs compute, not human hours. Real-world teleoperation, no matter how well organized, is bounded by the number of robots, operators, and hours in a day. If we believe embodied intelligence needs data on the scale that language models had, it's hard to see how we get there with real data alone.

But the practical limits are real, and I'd group them into three layers.

The first is perception. Visual sim-to-real used to be a huge problem. Rendering has improved a lot, and with domain randomization, depth sensing, or point clouds, the visual gap has become much more manageable, especially for grasping and pick-and-place. I'd say this layer is largely solvable now.

The second, and much harder, is physics. Rigid-body contact is okay. Once you get into deformable objects, cloth, cables, liquids, or tight insertion with high friction sensitivity, the simulator's model of the world starts to diverge from reality in ways that randomization alone can't cover. If the simulator gets the contact dynamics qualitatively wrong, the policy learns a strategy that simply doesn't exist in the real world. For contact-rich, dexterous manipulation, this is still the main ceiling.

The third is content and diversity. People underestimate this. A simulator is only as good as the objects, scenes, and tasks you put into it. Building millions of realistic, physically annotated assets with correct mass, articulation, and material properties is itself a big engineering problem. Generative models for 3D assets are helping, but we're not fully there.

So my practical view is that synthetic data is the backbone for pretraining: grasping, navigation, mobile manipulation, the broad generalizable skills. You use it to get coverage across objects, poses, lighting, and layouts that you could never collect in reality. Then you use a relatively small amount of high-quality real data to align and fine-tune, especially for the long tail of tasks where physics fidelity matters most.

In our own work, for things like dexterous grasping across many object categories, we've seen policies trained almost entirely in simulation transfer zero-shot with quite high success rates. That convinced me the "sim is useless" view is outdated. At the same time, I won't claim we can fold laundry purely from simulation today. The honest answer is that the limit isn't fixed. It moves as simulators, asset generation, and our understanding of what to randomize improve. A big part of our job is pushing that boundary forward.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I'd say the question is a bit different from how people usually frame it. People ask "does sim-to-real work," and the honest answer is that it works extremely well for some things and almost not at all for others, and the dividing line is pretty clear once you've spent time on it.

The thing that transfers best is geometry. If your task is dominated by where things are and what shape they have, like grasping rigid objects, placing, pushing, opening drawers, then synthetic data is a huge win. We can render millions of point clouds with perfect labels, randomize object poses and scenes, and a policy trained on that will generalize to real objects it has never seen. That's not speculation anymore, that's been demonstrated by many groups including ours. The reason is that depth sensors give you geometry fairly directly, so the gap between a simulated point cloud and a real one is mostly noise, and noise you can model.

Where it breaks down is contact physics and anything deformable. The moment the task depends on friction, on how a cable bends, on how a cloth drapes, on what happens when a cup slides a few millimeters during a grasp, the simulator is lying to you in ways you can't easily randomize away. You can domain-randomize friction coefficients, but the real problem is that the contact model itself is wrong, not just the parameters. So a policy that looks perfect in simulation does something subtly stupid in the real world, and you can't tell why from the simulator because the simulator agrees with the policy.

The second limit is perception beyond geometry. Transparent objects, reflective objects, lighting, textures, these are where RGB-based pipelines suffer badly, and rendering alone doesn't close that gap unless you're doing very expensive photorealistic rendering, which then stops scaling.

So the practical conclusion I've come to is a layered view. Use synthetic data to solve the parts of the problem that are essentially about geometry and coverage, because that's where simulation gives you orders of magnitude more diversity than you could ever collect by hand. Then use a small amount of real data, or real-world interaction, to correct the parts that simulation cannot represent faithfully. The mistake is believing either extreme: that you can do everything in sim, or that sim is useless and you should just teleoperate for a year. The real question is always which part of the task is your bottleneck, and matching the data source to that.

And I'd add one more thing. The limits are moving. Three years ago I would have said dexterous in-hand manipulation is firmly on the "doesn't transfer" side. Now with better contact simulation and hand hardware it's borderline. So I'd treat the boundary as a current state, not a law of nature.

astra-6.text:
I think the practical limit is less about how much synthetic data you can generate and more about whether that data captures the factors that determine success in the real world.

For manipulation, appearance is only one part of the gap. You also have contact, friction, compliance, sensor noise, and errors in control. A policy might recognize an object correctly and still fail because the object slips differently from what the simulator predicts. Those errors become especially important in tasks that require precise contact or handling deformable objects.

So I would treat synthetic data as a way to reduce the amount of real-world experience you need. You can use it to learn broad skills and expose the robot to variation, then use real-world trials to identify and correct the remaining gaps. Randomizing simulation parameters helps, but only if the variation covers what actually matters for the task.

The test is whether the robot succeeds reliably across objects and conditions you didn’t tune for—and whether it can detect and recover from a mistake. A successful demonstration shows that transfer is possible. Consistent performance tells you whether it is practical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the practical limit is that success in simulation doesn’t automatically mean you’ve learned the right behavior for the real world. You may have learned to exploit something about the simulator.

For manipulation, we need to distinguish visual transfer from physical transfer. You can randomize lighting, textures, camera positions, and object appearance, and that helps with perception. But contact is much harder. Small differences in friction, geometry, compliance, or the timing of the controller can determine whether an object slips or a grasp succeeds. Those differences become especially important in tasks like insertion or manipulating deformable objects.

So I would treat synthetic data as a way to get broad coverage and reduce the amount of real-world data you need. I wouldn’t assume it can eliminate real-world data altogether. A practical approach is to learn an initial policy in simulation, test it on the robot, identify the failures, and use those failures to improve either the simulation or the policy.

The key question is whether the synthetic data captures the variations that actually matter for the task. More simulated data is useful only if it prepares the robot for the uncertainty it will encounter in reality.

r001.rationale: Identifies physical contact differences—such as friction, geometry, compliance, and controller timing—as harder transfer obstacles than visual differences.

r002.rationale: Does not compare manipulation with robot walking or attribute walking transfer success to simpler contact physics.

r003.rationale: Mentions deformable-object tasks generally, but does not discuss shoelace tying or simulators’ inability to reproduce its complex contact dynamics.

r004.rationale: Does not present limiting a commercial robot’s task scope as a way to work around simulation limitations.
